title: Six client sentences, and what to ask
objectives: Match the six most common client sentences to the question that changes the advice.
Explain why each cause has a different fix.
body_md:
Clients rarely describe the real problem. These six sentences cover most of what you will hear.

| Client says | Ask | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| "I want to stop my SIP." | Is it cash flow, a market fall, a goal change or fund doubts? | Each cause has a different fix |
| "My SIP has ended. Now what?" | How far away is the goal? Is the goal amount still right? | Years away: renew. Near: start a glide path. Reached: plan withdrawals |
| "I got a raise / bonus." | Has the emergency fund been topped up? Any loans or near-term needs? | Step up only after basics are covered |
| "I need the money next year." | Exact date and amount? Any flexibility? | A short horizon means moving out of equity on a plan now |
| "I've retired." | Monthly expense need? Other income? | Sets the SWP amount and the safety buffer |
| "My SIP failed this month." | Mandate or balance issue? How many in a row? | Three consecutive misses (monthly) cancel the SIP |

## The habit behind the table

Every row is the same move: turn a request into a question, and a question into a plan. The client hears that you took the request seriously; you get the information that decides the answer.
example: Mr. Iyer says, "I've retired." The follow-up questions give a monthly need of ₹45,000 and a pension of ₹12,000 — so the plan covers the gap, not the whole amount, and keeps a one-year buffer in a liquid fund.
say: Let's start with what the money is for and when you need it.
How many instalments have failed in a row? That decides whether the SIP survives.
never: I've processed the stop as you asked.
A failed debit is nothing to worry about.

talk_track.title: When the client says…, ask…
talk_track.text: Here are the six things clients say most often, and what to ask. “I want to stop my SIP”: ask whether it's cash flow, a market fall, a change in goal, or doubts about the fund. “My SIP has ended”: ask how far away the goal is and whether the target is still right. “I got a raise”: ask whether the emergency fund is topped up and whether there are loans. “I need the money next year”: ask the exact date and amount. “I've retired”: ask about the monthly need and other income. And “my SIP failed”: ask how many in a row, because three in a row cancels a monthly SIP.

check.q: A client says, "I want to stop my SIP." What is the first move?
o: Ask whether it is cash flow, a market fall, a goal change or fund doubts
check.why: The cause decides the fix: pause for cash flow, stay for a fall, re-plan for a goal change, review the fund for doubts.

check.q: A client gets a raise and wants a bigger SIP. What comes first?
o: Step up by the whole raise immediately
Check the emergency fund and any costly loans
Stop the old SIP and start fresh
Invest the raise as a lump sum in a sectoral fund
check.why: Step up only after basics are covered. A step-up the client cannot sustain is the first thing cancelled.

check.q: A client needs the money in 12 months. What should the plan be?
o: Stay fully in equity until the money is needed
Move out of equity on a plan now
Add a small-cap fund for extra return
check.why: A short horizon means moving out of equity on a plan now, not at the last minute.
